$comment: Expected piece roster. This file — not the filesystem — is the source of truth for which pieces SHOULD exist; the build diffs it against src/ to produce each manifest's missing[] list. Declaring a piece before the artwork exists is the correct way to record a known gap. Set "individual": true on a family to also emit one file per piece alongside the sheet — for families like cards, where you show one face at a time and loading the whole sheet to do it would be wasteful. Default (omitted) is atlas-only: both Pixi and DOM read the single sheet.

board.description: Board surface textures and hand-drawn board lines
board.$note: No sourceSize: deliberately mixed-resolution. dark-tile is a 128x128 tile; squiggle-dash is a 74x4 strip tiled along each board line; hex-solid is a 302x348 closed hexagon outline. Shared rather than game-scoped because board furniture is not any one game's art -- go draws the squiggle today and any board can. The Pixi renderer rotates one strip per line, so it needs no separate vertical variant; the DOM .squiggle-border in design-system-tokens does, because CSS cannot rotate a background image. hex-solid is per-FACE art, not per-edge: a closed outline cannot feed latticeStrokes, so drawFaceSprites places one sprite per cell. Its master is pointy-top and drawFaceSprites rotates it for flat-top boards -- the same call the strip makes. The -half- variants carry only three contiguous edges, so a tiling draws each shared edge once instead of twice; the other half is the same file rotated 180 degrees, which the renderer does itself. Both were cut from their whole counterpart with a straight mask along the line joining the upper-right and lower-left vertices, so their two ends are sliced flat rather than drawn -- deliberate, and the thing to revisit if the joins ever read wrong at large scale. NOTE the solid and dashed masters do NOT share a canvas: hex-solid is 302x348 with the ink flush to the edges, hex-dash is 304x353 with a little padding, and their stroke centrelines sit at different fractions of the canvas (0.9754 vs 0.9641). The renderer carries one fit constant per master for that reason; a single shared one would draw the dashed board 1.2% small and open a gap at every shared edge. Exporting future variants from the same artboard would remove the need.  naming the variant now is what stops a bare `hex` needing a coordinated rename the day the dashed art lands.

fx.description: Generic decorative particles, shared across games.
fx.$note: Only art proven to be used by more than one game lives here. The three puffs are byte-identical between the chess and go visualizers, which is what earns them a place in a shared family.

chess-fx.description: Chess's own motion particles. Not reusable — several are piece silhouettes.
chess-fx.$note: Game-scoped on purpose. rook1-4, bishop1-2, pawn and knight-shadow are silhouettes of chess pieces; squiggle-1..3 are the king trail. Naming these generically would invite another game to import a rook outline as "decoration".

go.description: Go stones, markers and territory overlays
go.$note: No sourceSize: this family is deliberately mixed-resolution. The stones are 256×256 masters, the shadow 128, markers 88, territory marks 84 and hoshi 48. Every piece is drawn to a size that suits its job and is scaled at render time, so declaring one ratio for the family would be a lie the build would enforce. The three capture puffs are NOT here — they are byte-identical to chess's and live in the shared `fx` family.

card.$note: targets:["dom"] + atlas:false — every card game here (gin_rummy, bridge_arena, repeated_poker) is DOM and shows a hand at a time, so per-card files are the right shape. If a Pixi card game ever appears, add "pixi" to targets and set atlas:true: all 54 fit one 4096 sheet at 419x583 (9x7=63 slots, 91% of source), so this is a downscale decision, not a multi-page one.
